qt: to the Commission Dietmar Köster (S&D), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Pietro Bartolo (S&D), Damien Carême (Verts/ALE), Cornelia Ernst (The Left) Subject:

In July 2023, the Commission signed a memorandum of understanding on a partnership with Tunisia that includes migration. In it, the EU endeavours to take appropriate measures to facilitate legal mobility, including facilitating the granting of visas by reducing delays and costs. Can the Commission explain what these measures are, given that some Member States have reduced the number of Schengen visas allotted to Tunisian citizens, and that most of the costs are due to fees charged by third-party companies that are subcontracted by Member State embassies?
at: (English version) to the Commission Dietmar Köster (S&D), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Pietro Bartolo (S&D), Damien Carême (Verts/ALE), Cornelia Ernst (The Left) (9 February 2024) Subject: Memorandum of understanding with Tunisia In July 2023, the Commission signed a memorandum of understanding on a partnership with Tunisia that includes migration. In it, the EU endeavours to take appropriate measures to facilitate legal mobility, including facilitating the granting of visas by reducing delays and costs. Can the Commission explain what these measures are, given that some Member States have reduced the number of Schengen visas allotted to Tunisian citizens, and that most of the costs are due to fees charged by third-party companies that are subcontracted by Member State embassies? (2 May 2024) The Commission is committed to the EU-Tunisia memorandum of understanding on a strategic and global partnership signed on 16 July 2023 (1) and its implementation is underway. The joint objective is to address migration and mobility in order to harness the benefits of migration in economic and social development, to bring peoples closer together and to address the root causes of irregular migration. The Commission is informed about the difficulties faced by visa applicants in Tunisia and is working to improve access of Tunisian nationals to Schengen visa applications, in particular through better information and local adaptations of the general rules contained in the Visa Code (2), which governs the processing of visa applications. This work is ongoing. The Commission is not informed of any limitations in the number of visas issued to Tunisian nationals. As the visas examination relies on an individual assessment of each application based on its own merits, any limitation in the number of visas issued would be in contradiction with the Visa Code. In addition to the visa fee, applicants must pay a service fee to external service providers subcontracted by Member States to collect visa applications. This practice is tightly regulated in the Visa Code. In principle, the service fee cannot exceed half of the visa fee i.e. EUR 40.

https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_3887 Articles 14.5a and 24.2b of regulation 810/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 July 2009 establishing a Community Code on Visas.
